name: keras
title: Keras: The Multi-Backend Deep Learning API for Python
answer: Keras is an open source deep learning API for Python, maintained by the Keras team and released under the Apache 2.0 licence. It sits at the model-building layer of the AI stack, offering layers, losses, optimizers and training loops that run on top of JAX, TensorFlow, PyTorch or OpenVINO. The one thing to know before adopting it is that Keras 3 is a rewrite: code using only built-in layers and keras.ops moves between backends, while custom components tied to one framework's internals may need rework.

sections.body: Keras is a deep learning library for Python, described on its own site as deep learning for humans, made by the Keras team and hosted at github.com/keras-team/keras under the Apache 2.0 licence. It occupies the model definition and training layer of the AI stack: you describe a network as a stack of layers, then compile it with a loss, an optimizer and metrics, then call fit, evaluate or predict. It does not provide its own tensor runtime. Since Keras 3, announced on keras.io, the same workflows run on top of JAX, TensorFlow, PyTorch, or OpenVINO for inference only, so Keras sits above those engines rather than replacing them. The repository shows steady activity, with a last push in October 2026 and roughly 64,000 stars.
sections.heading: What it is and where it sits in AI work

sections.body: The official guides show Keras used for the ordinary work of deep learning: image classification on MNIST, autoencoders built with the functional API, transfer learning on a flower dataset, and a scaled down GPT trained from scratch with KerasHub for text generation. Training, evaluation and inference follow the same calls whether a model is Sequential, built with the functional API, or written by subclassing, and the built-in loops accept NumPy arrays, tf.data.Dataset objects, PyTorch DataLoader objects and Pandas dataframes regardless of backend. Keras is strongest where you want one readable codebase across frameworks, and where built-in layers cover the architecture. The site notes that JAX typically gives the best training and inference performance on GPU, TPU and CPU, though results vary by model, and non-XLA TensorFlow is occasionally faster on GPU.
sections.heading: What it is used for and where it is strongest

sections.body: The learning curve is gentle by deep learning standards. You need working Python, and some familiarity with tensors and neural network concepts helps, but the guides start from loading MNIST and reshaping arrays to float32 before dividing by 255, so no advanced mathematics is assumed up front. The Sequential guide explains that layers need to know their input shape before they can create weights, and that a model without an input shape is not built and has no weights, which is the kind of practical detail beginners hit early. The official site offers guides on the Sequential model, the functional API and built-in training methods, plus runnable examples, which is enough for a newcomer to train a first model without leaving the documentation.
sections.heading: How hard it is to learn and what you need first

sections.body: Keras 3 implements the full Keras API across TensorFlow, JAX and PyTorch, including over a hundred layers, dozens of metrics, loss functions, optimizers, callbacks, training and evaluation loops, and saving and serialization infrastructure. The keras.ops namespace provides backend-agnostic operations such as matmul, sum, stack and einsum, along with neural network functions like softmax, binary_crossentropy and conv, so custom layers written against it work on all three backends. KerasHub supplies pretrained models and layers, used in the site's mini-GPT example. The site claims over 2.5 million developers have chosen Keras, and the repository's star count and recent commit activity indicate a live project, though the site does not break that figure down by region or use case.
sections.heading: Ecosystem and community

sections.body: Keras is built for both, with a trade-off in how much control you take. The Sequential and functional APIs, the compile and fit loop, and utilities like plot_model make short experiments quick, and the site's examples train small models in a couple of epochs. For production, Keras 3 adds a distribution API in the keras.distribution namespace, currently implemented for the JAX backend with TensorFlow and PyTorch promised, covering model parallelism, data parallelism and combinations of both. A Keras model can be instantiated as a PyTorch Module, exported as a TensorFlow SavedModel, or used as a stateless JAX function. The cost is that backend-specific tuning, such as XLA settings or custom kernels, sits outside the portable surface, and the site does not claim Keras matches hand-tuned framework code in every case.
sections.heading: Prototyping speed against production performance

sections.body: The site states that Keras powers systems including the Waymo self-driving fleet and the YouTube recommendation engine, and that over 2.5 million developers have chosen it. Those are the adoption claims the official material makes, and it does not publish a breakdown by industry or company size. For someone choosing what to learn, Keras is a current standard rather than a legacy choice: Keras 3 is the released version, the repository is actively maintained, and the multi-backend design means skills transfer to JAX, TensorFlow and PyTorch work. The site does not discuss salaries, job titles or hiring demand, so any career judgement beyond the framework's continued relevance would go past what the facts support.
sections.heading: Industry adoption and careers

sections.body: Keras is a Python library, and the polyglot pattern it belongs to is one where a high-level model API sits over a lower-level tensor engine. In Keras 3 that engine can be JAX, TensorFlow or PyTorch, and OpenVINO is supported for inference only. The site describes Keras as usable as a low-level cross-framework language for custom components such as layers, models or metrics that then run in native JAX, TensorFlow or PyTorch workflows from one codebase. Existing tf.keras models that use only built-in layers can start running in JAX and PyTorch right away. The site does not describe integrations with non-Python languages, so Keras should be read as a Python-first layer in a Python-centric stack.
sections.heading: How it fits beside the others

sections.body: The clearest limit is portability of custom code. The site says any Keras model using only built-in layers works immediately on all supported backends, and that custom layers work across JAX, PyTorch and TensorFlow as long as they use only keras.ops, which implies that components reaching into a specific framework's internals do not travel. The distribution API is implemented for JAX only, with TensorFlow and PyTorch support described as coming soon, so large-scale training on those backends is less settled. The site does not state a release cadence, a long-term support policy, or how the 2.5 million developer figure was measured, and it gives no guidance on when Keras is the wrong choice compared with using a backend framework directly.
sections.heading: Limits and open questions
